title: The dome and the minaret
hookLine: the dome as the sky, the minaret as the voice

cards: Before the towers, there was a roof. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud tells of a woman whose house stood beside the mosque of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in Medina.

Hers, she said, was one of the tallest houses around it. Before dawn, Bilal would come, climb up, and sit on her roof, watching for first light. When he saw it, he stood and called the people to prayer.

A neighbor's rooftop, a man watching the sky, and a voice. Later, cities would raise towers for that voice, and lift great round roofs over the people praying underneath. Today: the dome and the minaret.

teach.b: Take the minaret first, because it is the voice. Its job is to carry the adhan, the call to prayer, over the rooftops: God is greatest, come to prayer, come to success.

Minarets take many shapes: square towers in Morocco, the spiral stair you met at Ibn Tulun's mosque, pencil-thin towers in Istanbul. The job is the same: lift a human voice so the whole neighborhood can hear.
Today a loudspeaker often does the lifting, and the tower still stands like a finger pointing up: the call comes from here. Now the dome, which is the sky. Stand underneath one and look up.
The walls stop being walls and curve over you, gathering toward one point overhead.

teach.h: THE DOME IS A SKY INDOORS.
teach.b: Inside, a dome may be painted with stars, patterns and verses, like a heaven brought indoors.
The Qur'an speaks of God, in Pickthall's words, as the one "Who hath appointed the earth a resting-place for you, and the sky a canopy." A dome is a canopy you can stand under.
Put them together and a mosque makes two gestures.

teach.h: ONE GATHERS IN, ONE SENDS OUT.
teach.b: The dome gathers people in. The minaret sends a voice out. And neither one is required.

teach.h: MUD BRICK AND PALM IN MEDINA.
teach.b: A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari describes the Prophet's own mosque as mud brick, with a roof of palm leaves and pillars of palm trunks. A mosque can be a rented room with no dome and no tower.
Prayer needs a clean place and a direction. The dome and the minaret are what love for that prayer built on top of it.

how: Muslims hear the adhan from minarets, often through loudspeakers now, and pray under domes in many large mosques; plenty of mosques, from storefronts to village prayer rooms, have neither.

o: a loudspeaker mounted on a mosque's outer wall
the round roof that curves over a prayer hall
the tower that lifts the call to prayer over a town

s: a mosque must have a dome and a minaret

Bilal called the dawn prayer from a neighbor's rooftop
a hadith in Abu Dawud tells of a woman whose house was among the tallest near the mosque.
the Prophet's mosque in Medina had a great dome

games.q: you're Bilal before dawn in Medina. there's no tower yet. how do you make sure the call reaches everyone?
o: climb a tall house nearby and wait for first light.
games.why: the hadith in Abu Dawud says he sat on a neighbor's roof, one of the tallest houses around the mosque, watched for dawn, then stood and called.

practice: Look up: at a dome if there's one near you, or a ceiling, the open sky, or one you remember with your eyes closed, and rest under the curve. Then listen for any voice calling, near or far.
If you pray, you can remember the first words of the call, God is greatest; if you don't, just rest there.

wordCard.voice: Minaret. The tower that lifts the call to prayer, paired with the dome, a sky you can stand under. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a minaret, the place of the call.
